title: Spirulina vs. chlorella: what is the difference?

seo.title: Spirulina vs. chlorella: key differences
seo.meta_description: Spirulina and chlorella are both protein-rich green powders, but one is a cyanobacterium and the other a green microalga. Compare cell walls, pigments, B12, and nutrition.
seo.search_intent: Compare spirulina and chlorella and understand their practical nutritional differences

excerpt: Spirulina is a filamentous cyanobacterium; chlorella is a single-celled green microalga. Both can provide roughly 50–70% protein by dry weight, but chlorella has a tougher cell wall that often needs disruption for digestibility. B12 also differs: spirulina is dominated by inactive analogs, while some chlorella products contain active B12, with substantial variability.
content_html:
Spirulina and chlorella are sold as nearly interchangeable green powders, but they are biologically different organisms. Spirulina is a cyanobacterium; chlorella is a eukaryotic green microalga.

Both can be very high in protein

Reviews place both spirulina and Chlorella vulgaris in roughly the 50–70% protein-by-dry-weight range under some growing conditions. Both contain essential amino acids.

Serving size still matters. A 5 g powder that is 60% protein provides about 3 g protein, regardless of how striking the percentage looks on a dry-weight chart.

Cell walls create a practical difference

Spirulina lacks the tough cellulose-rich wall associated with many green microalgae. Chlorella has a more resistant cell wall that can reduce access to intracellular nutrients.

That is why products often advertise “cracked cell wall” chlorella. Mechanical disruption is intended to improve nutrient accessibility rather than merely change texture.

The pigments are different

Spirulina is famous for blue phycocyanin alongside chlorophyll, giving it a blue-green color. Chlorella is especially chlorophyll-rich and appears a more straightforward deep green.

Pigment concentration can be interesting technologically and nutritionally, but color is not a clinical health score.

Vitamin B12 is not the same story

Inactive B12 analogs dominate in spirulina. Some studied chlorella products have contained biologically active cobalamin, but amounts differ with strain, culture, and product.

Anyone depending on B12—especially on a vegan diet—should use a source with a dependable labeled dose instead of assuming all chlorella supplies enough.

Other nutrients depend heavily on the product

Iron, carotenoids, fatty acids, and minerals vary with species, growth medium, harvest, and drying. Comparing two actual labels is often more meaningful than declaring one generic powder nutritionally superior.

Which should you choose?

Both can add protein in small amounts. Spirulina generally needs less cell-wall processing; chlorella has its own pigment profile and some products may provide active B12 measured specifically.

There is no universal winner. Manufacturing quality, testing, dose, and what you want from the product matter more than the “superfood” category.

faq.question: Are spirulina and chlorella the same algae?
faq.answer: No. Spirulina is a cyanobacterium; chlorella is a single-celled green microalga.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Both can reach roughly 50–70% protein by dry weight, so product-specific data are more useful than naming a universal winner.

faq.question: Why does chlorella say 'cracked cell wall'?
faq.answer: Its tougher cell wall can limit nutrient accessibility, so processing is used to disrupt it.

faq.question: Which is a reliable B12 source?
faq.answer: Spirulina is not. Some chlorella products contain active B12, but amounts vary; use a verified source if B12 intake depends on it.
